items.title: PM Carney: ‘You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.’ Live trade war updates.

items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. President Donald Trump’s new 50 per cent tariffs amount to an economic “attack” on Canada. He has vowed “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8.

  • Trade War Coverage on CTVNews.ca

His remarks come after a late-night decision to call off trade talks with the U.S. He says last-minute requests from the American delegation led to a breakdown in negotiations, and that Canada is at economic “war” with the U.S.

Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs target US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement and hockey sticks.

Follow for key updates:

Canada ‘at war?’

Carney was asked: “Why does it feel like, today, Mark Carney is going to war, trade war?”

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he responded.

He said Canada had waited for the U.S. to implement tariffs to respond this way, and now that they have, “we’ve got the reserves. We’ve got the resilience”

“We’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus,” he continued. “We’re going to focus on what we can control. We’re going to build.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Retaliatory tariffs to come after Labour Day

Carney said retaliatory tariffs, in response to Trump’s new levies, will come into force on Sept. 8.

In his address on Saturday, Carney acknowledged that the tariffs will “raise costs and reduce choice” for Canadians.

But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada, and that by rejecting a bad deal by standing up for Canada, (we focus) on what we can control,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Kinew stands with Carney, vows to fight back

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says he fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.

Speaking Saturday afternoon, Kinew commended the prime minister for standing up for Canadians and that all premiers are united with Carney.

“History will not be kind to Donald Trump. So we should never appease him and we should fight back, which is what Canada is doing today,” said Kinew. “We can fight back against Donald Trump by buying from Canadian businesses, by supporting Canadian workers and most importantly, by living up to our Canadian values.”

Devon McKendrick, CTV News Winnipeg Editorial Producer

Read the full story here.

U.S. tariffs are violation of CUSMA deal, Sask. premier says

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is calling new U.S. tariffs a violation of the CUSMA trade deal.

“Last minute changes by U.S. negotiators undermined the fairness and reliability of the deal,” Moe said in an X post on Saturday.

Moe says over the past few days, the Canadian government was working toward a deal that would have avoided new tariffs and reduced some tariffs that were previously imposed by the U.S.

“The new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on some Canadian goods are a clear violation of CUSMA and a clear indication that the current U.S. administration cannot be trusted to live up to its own trade deals,” Moe’s statement read.

Caitlin Brezinski, Digital Journalist, CTV News Regina

Read the full story here

U.S. proposals would turn Canada into 51st state: Eby

B.C. Premier David Eby says a request from U.S. negotiators would have effectively reduced Canada to America’s 51st state.

“The suggestion that Canada would not trade with other countries or reduce our trade with other countries because the Americans tell us to would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state,” said Eby, fresh from a meeting with Carney, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and other premiers.

Earlier today, Carney was asked for specifics on what he called new and “economically unfair” terms proposed by American negotiators.

He said the U.S. had made efforts to “restrict our ability to have other trade deals” in the last hours of trade talks.

“The prime minister and his team rightly walked away from any suggestion that we would agree to that,” said Eby.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Read the full story here.

North ready to create jobs: NWT premier

The premier of Northwest Territories says the North is ready to create jobs, strengthen Canadian supply chains, open new markets and make Canada more self-reliant.

R.J. Simpson says Canada tried to negotiate with the U.S. government in good faith, and the prime minister was right to walk away from trade talks rather than accept a deal at any cost.

Simpson says Canada can build its economic strength at home and N.W.T. is a big part of the nation-building work that’s coming.

Canada after ‘win-win’ partnership

Executive Director of the Independent Wood Processors Association in B.C. Brian Menzies says he is “concerned” about the 50 per cent tariffs on the wood industry.

Speaking to CTV News Channel Saturday, he said companies will shortly have to make decisions about continuing their operations and keeping people employed.

Menzies said Canada is a country that wants a “win-win” relationship with its trade partners, adding that if our customers and partners in the United States don’t win, “we don’t win.”

He said Canada is on the “right track” by keeping that principle in mind, and that the wood industry must now transition to other markets and will need some help adjusting to that.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Wine industry benefiting from tariffs a ‘myth’

President of Wine Growers Canada Dan Paszkowski says the tariff war is destroying markets that have taken the Canadian wine industry decades to make.

In an interview with CTV News Channel, he said Canada cannot “control what Washington does but we can strengthen the Canadian wine industry” through federal investment programs.

Paszkowski said that “would provide us with a lot of certainty.”

He noted that investment is especially important because in three to four weeks, wine growers will start harvesting for this year, but added there is currently no support for that.

Paszkowski highlighted that it would be helpful if provincial and federal officials made it easy for “Canadians to find Canadian wine.”

He also said the Canadian wine industry benefiting from the tariffs is a “myth.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Mark Carney chairs first ministers’ meeting

The Prime Minister’s Office says Mark Carney met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers Saturday to discuss the suspension of trade negotiations with the United States.

The PMO says Carney outlined next steps to protect Canadian interests, including dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs that will take effect on the Tuesday after Labour Day, along with additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses affected by U.S. tariffs.

Carney also emphasized the importance of a united “Team Canada” approach, with continued collaboration between the federal, provincial and territorial governments on nation-building projects, diversifying export markets and removing internal trade barriers.

Tammy Ibrahimpour, CTV News National Digital Producer

Canada avoided a ‘chokehold’

International trade analyst and government affairs specialist at Gowling WLG Jacques Shore says by walking away from the tariff talks, Canada has avoided a “chokehold.”

In an interview with CTV News Channel, Shore described the situation as a “missed opportunity” for the United States.

He said the last-minute conditions put forward in the talks by the U.S. were “surprising.”

Shore highlighted that it would be hard to imagine that “we would be restricted from engaging with other countries” and making decisions that are only Canada’s to make.

He said despite these “trade tensions,” Canada and the U.S. are integrated and will be working together.

Shore added that, at this point, there are “Americans who are scratching their heads wondering how this could have happened to Canada.”He said this will “harm the American economy,” but Canada alsohas to brace itself.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

F bombs in a trade war

California Governor Gavin Newsom made his feelings clear on social media Saturday morning.

“Our closest ally. Our critical trading partner. And Trump is hitting Canada with 50% tariffs,” wrote Newsom on X. “What the actual f--- are we doing?”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Deal would have not brought back auto jobs to Brampton: mayor

Patrick Brown, the mayor of Brampton, Ont., also commended the prime minister’s decision not to accept a bad deal and to match the new U.S. tariffs.

“This is not a trade war that we have asked for. Unfortunately, we’re in it because of the misguided policies of Donald Trump. But it doesn’t mean we should take it lying down,” Brown said in an interview with CP24 on Saturday afternoon.

“When I hear the premier and the prime minister say tariff for tariff, it’s our only recourse. We can’t continue to be bullied by this president.”

He noted that the reported terms of the deal that included permanent tariffs on the auto sector wouldn’t have brought the jobs at the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant, which has been idling since 2023.

Last week, Unifor claimed that Stellantis was seriously considering closing and selling the plant.

“Stellantis made it clear to me that as long as there are tariffs, there was no business case for auto production in Canada, and they were leaving until tariffs were lifted. So, I’m glad the prime minister didn’t accept a bad deal,” Brown said.

“It would not have salvaged the auto sector in Canada.”

Bryann Aguilar, CP24.com/CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Uncertainty better than certainty around a bad deal’

President and CEO of Global Automakers of Canada Lucas Malinowski believes it’s “unfortunate” that the U.S. and Canada couldn’t come to an agreement regarding the auto industry.

In an interview with CTV News Channel, he said the North American auto sector has incurred $110 billion in tariff-related costs over the past year and a half, making the industry “less competitive” and cars “more expensive” for consumers.

Yet, he admitted that, at the end of the day, “uncertainty is still better than certainty around a bad deal.”

Malinowski also said the deal on the table was “untenable,” based on Prime Minister Carney’s remarks and what the government has said.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Two-year root canal’ ahead for Canadians, Sarnia mayor says

Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley says Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision regarding the tariff talks was “100 per cent” correct but admits “the tough stuff” will now start.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration will “search and destroy” every relationship it has around the world in the next two years, including ties with Canada, he said in an interview with CTV News Channel. “Canadians need to stand together.”

Bradley said the situation for Canadians will be like a “permanent root canal for the next year or two,” but added that “it will be worth it.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘There are no deals’ with Trump: Former Harper aide

Former Director of Communications to Stephen Harper Kory Teneycke believes Prime Minister Mark Carney should prepare the nation for an “incredibly difficult period of time,” but supports Canada’s approach in the tariff talks.

In an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV News Channel, he said that if there is one thing we’ve learned from U.S. President Donald Trump, it’s that “there are no deals.”

Teneycke described Trump as a president who “has broken every agreement he has made on every topic” since he took office.

“He is the kind of guy who starts bombing you when you’re in peace talks,” he said, adding that Canada didn’t start this war, but “we’re going to be there to finish it.”

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

No deal was ‘surprising’: trade lawyer

Greg Kanargelidis, an international trade lawyer, said not reaching an agreement with the U.S. over the tariffs was “surprising”.

In an interview with CTV News Channel on Saturday, he said, “it was surprising to hear… about talks collapsing.”He said Canadian importers will be impacted by tariffs, but they could, in part, be compensated for through remissions orders.

The trade lawyer added that the tariffs will also impact a wide range of goods, including agricultural products, wood products, electronics, sporting goods, dairy and alcohol.

He noted the impact for companies in those industries will be “perhaps impossible to withstand.”.

Kanargelidis said the discussions could also serve as a “base” for CUSMA negotiations but admitted they may be at a “standstill” for the time being.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump ‘can’t be trusted’: Ford

Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticized U.S. President Donald Trump, portraying him as an untrustworthy bully whose tariff strategy harms both Canadians and Americans.

He says Trump “can’t be trusted” because “he changes the deal” and “keeps moving the goalpost.”

Speaking to reporters, Ford added that Trump is “the type of person that would steal your lunch money the first day, he’d steal the toque off your head the second day, and the third day he’d steal your running shoes.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘No deal is better than a bad deal’: Ford told Carney in letter

In a newly released letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged Ottawa to stand firm against the United States after President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs took effect following the collapse of last-minute trade talks.

The premier had largely remained quiet in recent days as negotiations continued.

However, in the letter, Ford told Carney that “no deal is better than a bad deal” that could encourage the United States to seek further concessions from Canada.

“We cannot allow arbitrary deadlines, shifting justifications or escalating tariff threats to weaken our resolve,” Ford wrote.

He said Ontario would not support removing its existing retaliatory measures without a deal that provides “significant relief” for Ontario workers, businesses and key sectors

Jermaine Wilson, CTVNews.ca Journalist

PM: U.S. proposed new ‘unfair’ terms

Carney said that progress was being made on negotiations towards a “mutually beneficial deal.” But in recent days, American negotiators proposed “new terms that were economically unfair.”

The terms “undermined net benefits for Canadians and called into question the reliability of any deal,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Last-minute changes

Carney was asked to specify what the U.S. sought to change in the final hours of negotiations.

Among those changes, he said the Americans had proposed a treatment of auto trade that was unacceptable to the Canadian team.

He also said the U.S. had taken “efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals,” and that “we believe in free trade.”

Carney was asked later if Canada had any of its own last-minute requests.

“’No’ is the short answer,” he responded.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Changes included auto, trade restrictions

The U.S. made “last-minute” requests to change the deal regarding the auto sector and Canada’s capacity to have other trade accords, according to Carney.

“The Americans wanted to limit it to autos only, not include medium and heavy duty trucks which is a big change, obviously,” he said.

Negotiators also introduced “at the last hour” efforts to restrict Canada’s ability to have other trade deals, he added.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Would Canada tariff other countries in co-ordination with U.S.?

When asked by a reporter if the U.S. expected Canada to tariff other countries as part of a trade deal, Carney responded, “there were elements of that.”

Canada could agree to that as part of an “integrated” market system with the U.S., Carney added.

But if that’s what the Americans are after, Carney said American tariffs on Canadian exports should be “clearly the lowest” among trading partners.

Asked why he thought the U.S. was interested in influencing Canadian foreign trade policy, Carney said “it’s a power play.”

Devika Desai and Luca Caruso-Moro,, CTVNews.ca journalist

B.C. Premier to address trade talks at 3 p.m. EDT

B.C. Premier David Eby will address the breakdown in trade talks in Vancouver at 3 p.m. EDT.

This follows the prime minister’s own remarks earlier today on the breakdown in negotiations between Canada and U.S. trade representatives shortly before the Trump’s tariff deadline expired.

In a social media post earlier today, Eby stated that “British Columbians will always stand with Canada.”

“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” his post reads.

Follow along for more information here.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Mastering energy is mastering destiny’

Carney said Canada has been putting efforts towards ‘mastering energy’ and becoming an independent superpower.

“We’ve doubled the capacity of our electrical network from (now) to 2050,” he said.

He referred to an announcement made on Monday by federal government, Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, to update and expand the Churchills Falls generating station, as well as develop the Gull island project and transmissions.

He described it as the “single largest investment in Canada’s history to build the largest clean energy project.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Canada investing local

Canada will invest $25 billion to protect workers and businesses affected by the tariffs, Carney said.

This will include investments in “equipment, productivity and supply chain resilience,” as well as financing large companies to keep employers “afloat,” he added.

“We’re helping those hardest hit industries retool and pivot to those new international markets, and we’re being our own best customers,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

PM: Tariffs will hit U.S. steel and dairy

Carney said the retaliatory tariffs will hit sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agriculture, electronics.

“Also include products that are currently subject to unjustified Section 232 tariffs. This is a focused response to protect and defend our industries and allow them to compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Premier pushback did not ‘factor’ in negotiations

Pushback from premiers in recent days over returning U.S. booze to stores did not factor into suspending trade negotiations, Carney said.

“The essence of (Wednesday’s meeting) was ... that we were on a path to a potential deal that would give Canadians ... the best deal in all our strategic sectors,” he said.

The price for that deal was “worth paying,” he added.

Last-minute changes by the Americans made the deal ‘uneconomic’, he added. “So we’re not asking the premiers to do anything.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Tariff protection for Canadians on its way

Carney said that tariff protection will be provided to business affected by the U.S. tariffs.

“Many of them are small, medium-sized businesses,” he said. “They’re in a wide range of industries spread across the country, concentrated (in) Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia.”

He did not say when the protections will be announced but added that it will be released “in a few days.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump tariffs ‘deeply troubling’: Business CEO

The CEO of a national business non-profit called the tariffs “deeply troubling” for thousands of small Canada businesses.

“A full 40 per cent of small exporters sell items on the new 10+ page list of items facing 50 per cent tariffs. Many CFIB members have said this will end their U.S. sales, and some have reported this will kill their businesses,” Dan Kelly, president and CEO of the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses said.

“I hope that discussions continue and an interim deal can be quickly found.”

Read more here on how people are responding after the U.S. tariffs came into effect on Saturday.

Devika Desai CTVNews.ca journalist

Diversifying trade is ‘Plan A’

Carney said he will continue to focus on “building at home and diversifying trade abroad.”

“It has been our Plan A from the start,” he said.“Canada will continue to pursue this path to build Canada strong because it’s right and because it’s working,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trouble in Steel City

Andrea Horwath, mayor of Hamilton, Ont., says the breakdown of tariff negotiations is extremely concerning.

She says Hamilton is a steel and manufacturing city with a large agricultural sector, and the uncertainty ahead will be stressful for many of its residents.

Horwath called on federal and provincial leaders to stand behind Canadian workers and industries.

Hamilton is responsible for approximately 60 per cent of Canada’s steel output.

Poilievre: Canada can’t accept one-way tariffs

“Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal,” reads a statement from Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre Saturday morning.

He said his party is disappointed with the Americans’ move to impose new tariffs, calling them “unjustified” and adding they “threaten the jobs and livelihoods of families right across our country.”

He also called on the Liberal government to end its industrial carbon levy and enact “major tax reforms” to spur investment, among other measures.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca Journalist

Premiers respond to failed trade talks

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the “prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”

B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, said Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.”

There is frustration, however, from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who says she is “deeply disappointed” that no deal was reached and is “urging the federal government to restart negotiations as soon as possible.”

Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager. Read the full story here.

Here is everything that happened on Aug. 21:

PM Carney says Canada intends to match the U.S. tariffs ‘dollar for dollar’

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office released a statement ahead of the deadline saying he suspended trade negotiations with the United States, setting in motion the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods.

“I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa. They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” the PMO said in the statement.

“However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

“At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods,” the statement read.

“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist

Canada has declined to finalize the trade deal, ‘upended’ balance: Greer

In a statement released Friday night, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada has declined to finalize the deal and “upended” the balance reached during the negotiations.

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” the statement said.

“In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services.”

The statement went on to say that Canada declined the deal despite the U.S. offering Canada “better treatment” and “significant tariff reductions” on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber in exchange for concessions.

“The U.S. offer was also forward-looking and included a historic economic and national security partnership to cooperate on export controls, combat transshipment, enhance digital trade, and align certain external tariffs,” Greer said in the statement.

“This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist

‘Tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar’: Ford extends support for prime minister

Ontario Premier Doug Ford extended his support for Prime Minister Mark Carney in a social media post, after the trade negotiations were suspended Friday night.

“Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before,” Ford said.

“The prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar. As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist

‘We’ll keep fighting’: Eby

B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, also responded to the news, saying Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.”

“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” Eby added.

Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager

As tariff deadline approaches, dynamic ‘not going well:’ sources

With less than two hours until new 50 per cent tariffs are set to be imposed on a variety of Canadian goods, two sources close to the negotiations tell CTV News that there are some challenges with the dynamic in negotiations, particularly with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick who is involved in the final hours of talks.

According to the sources, the talks are focused on “just a couple” of outstanding issues, but some of the personal dynamics with Lutnick, who appears to have lingering feelings over recent issues with the Gordie Howe International Bridge, is a challenge. The opening of the bridge was delayed for weeks because of U.S. complaints over toll governance and revenue sharing, after which Canada agreed to share revenues earlier than planned.

Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette remains at the United States Representative’s office in Washington as of late Friday night as talks continue.

Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager

With files from CTV’s Chief Political Correspondent Vassy Kapelos and CTV’s Senior Political Correspondent Mike Le Couteur

‘Working up until the last minute’: LeBlanc

“We have more work to do,” LeBlanc told reporters as he exited the U.S. trade representatives office around 7:30 p.m. on Friday.

“We’re going to continue working up until the last minute. Our job is not finished. Canadian workers, Canadian businesses expect us to do all of this important work” he said.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘I only make good deals,’ Trump says

“I only make good deals,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

He was asked about progress toward a deal with Canada. He said talks were “moving along,” and that his team has a “good relationship” with Carney.

He didn’t offer details on the prospective deal.

“We have to take care of our farmers.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

A ‘low-key horrible’ deal: trade policy expert

Some concern about the deal still persists, an international trade policy researcher told CTV News Channel.

“For some of the leaks we’ve seen, it doesn’t sound like it’s going to be a good deal,” Stuart Trew said hours before the deadline on Friday.

“In fact, as my niece might say, it sounds ‘pretty low-key horrible’” Trew said, referring to tariffs that will remain on steel exports to the U.S.

“Aluminum (and) the auto tariffs, at least according to the leaks, being at 15 per cent would be – in the short-to-medium term – pretty unsustainable for the industry.”

Trew said such a deal would inevitably “eat into the reason to make any vehicles in Canada whatsoever.”

He cautioned against putting Canada in a worse position than before the trade war started by accepting a deal that would put U.S. booze back on the shelves and letting go of our retaliatory tariffs.

“The legitimate question is why would we come to such a bad deal now, when all we’re getting out of this is some kind of barely noticeable reprieve, right?”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Aiming to get the best agreement’: Alberta’s Smith

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is optimistic for a new trade deal with the United States, telling CTV News Calgary the best deal for Canada would involve no additional tariffs.

“I know everybody hopes that we could get 100 per cent of all products going across the border tariff free,” Smith said in an interview.

“But I think where we’re at in the negotiations is that we’re aiming to get the best agreement in the world of any nation with the United States and a reduction in the current tariffs that we have.”

It’s the first time Smith has spoken on the intense negotiations between Ottawa and Washington during trade deadline week.

Cassidy McMackon, CTV News Calgary, Digital Producer

Compromise a ‘hallmark’ of any good deal: former U.S. ambassador to Canada

For any good deal, there need to be concessions on both sides, according to former U.S. ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen.

Cohen told CTV News Channel Friday night that he has been “optimistic,” throughout the process and that although it might take both, Canada and the U.S. some time to reach an agreement, there will ultimately be one.

However, he said the “hallmark” of a good deal is when there is “some unhappiness” on both sides.

“There’s a compromise here, and it’s a compromise where Canada is giving something up, but the U.S. is giving something up too,” Cohen said.

“Both sides giving something up, both sides being a little unhappy with the landing place, but both sides looking at the bigger picture and understanding that there are huge benefits to both Canada and the U.S. to a resolution of this dispute, which has not benefited either country.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist

Trade deal is an ‘economic security negotiation’: analyst

Following Trump’s comment that trade talks are moving along, an international trade analyst says securing a deal is now effectively an “economic security negotiation.”

“I feel for the number of companies, the factories, and all those that are engaged in looking at this carefully to ensure that they can continue to do business,” Jacques Shore told CTV News Channel on Friday.

Canada needs to reach a trade agreement “right now,” to ensure goods currently protected under CUSMA with no tariffs on them “remain as they are without this potential of 50 per cent,” Shore added.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump’s tariffs on autos ‘outrageous’: spokesperson

National spokesperson of the Canadian Automobile Dealers Association, Huw Williams believes that Canada and the U.S. should have completely automotive free trade as in the past 60 years but that must be viewed with a “dose of realism” that the other side is an unpredictable and “bombastic” administration.

items.title: Tesla teases imminent launch of Cybercab ‘robotaxi’
items.description: Electric vehicle-maker Tesla is teasing the upcoming debut of its self-driving robotaxi, dubbed “Cybercab,” to compete with the likes of Uber and Waymo.

items.body:
NEW YORK - Electric vehicle-maker Tesla is teasing the upcoming debut of its self-driving robotaxi, dubbed “Cybercab,” to compete with the likes of Uber and Waymo.

The Elon Musk-founded company shared a promotional image on social media late Friday promising “exclusive access” to Cybercabs at a September 3 event in Austin, Texas, where Tesla is headquartered.

“We’re celebrating the launch of our Cybercab robotaxi with an exclusive event in Austin -- and you could be there,” the company said on its website, promoting a sweepstakes to win a chance to attend the event.

First unveiled in October 2024, the gold-colored vehicle can carry two passengers and marks the first Tesla car with no steering wheel or pedals.

At the time, Musk said the company was planning to begin production of the self-driving cars before 2027 and sell them to private buyers for under US$30,000.

U.S. tech industry publication The Information reported this week that Tesla staffers have been told the rollout will begin with Cybercab rides for employees on public roads, followed by the vehicle being incorporated into the ranks of its Robotaxi service in Austin.

Tesla enthusiasts have in recent weeks reported seeing parking lots filled with Cybercabs, sparking rumors of an impending launch.

Last year Tesla debuted its self-driving cars in Austin using its Model Y SUV vehicles, with the “Robotaxi” service gradually expanding to several other cities in Texas, Florida and California.

However, state laws require many of the vehicles to have a human supervisor or driver ready to take over control if necessary.

Waymo, the self-driving vehicle subsidiary of Google parent company Alphabet, offers its services in 11 U.S. cities.

items.title: Ford wants Ontario to hit back after Trump’s latest tariffs on Canada
items.description: Ontario Premier Doug Ford is doubling down on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to suspend trade negotiations with the United States, saying Canada must respond forcefully after new U.S. tariffs took effect Saturday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney speak to reporters on Saturday Aug. 22, 2026.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Ontario Premier Doug Ford is doubling down on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to suspend trade negotiations with the United States, saying Canada must respond forcefully after new U.S. tariffs took effect Saturday.
items.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is doubling down on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to suspend trade negotiations with the United States, saying Canada must respond forcefully after new U.S. tariffs took effect Saturday.

“Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before,” Ford said in a post to social media late Friday. “The prime minister has my full support for a strong response — tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”

  • A list of items the U.S. is slapping with a 50 per cent tariff

The comments came after Carney suspended negotiations with the U.S. just minutes before a midnight deadline, saying last-minute changes proposed by Washington were “unfair, uneconomic” and raised questions about the reliability of any potential deal.

The United States has now imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods, including products such as cement and hockey sticks. Carney has pledged to match the measures “dollar for dollar.”

Here’s the latest from Ontario’s premier.

‘It was a bad deal’

Speaking to CP24, Ford framed the tariff dispute with the U.S. as an “economic war” and repeatedly stressed that Canada needs a united national response.

He says that he’s always said the country needs to fight “tariff to tariff, dollar to dollar.”

“We never started this fight, but I can assure you, we’re going to win this fight. We’re going to be united Team Canada,” Ford said.

He also defended rejecting the proposed deal as necessary to protect Ontario’s key industries: “I’m glad he didn’t sign that deal because it was a bad deal… for the auto sector, the steel sector, and manufacturing sector."

“I wasn’t prepared to put steel workers and auto workers… in uncertainty. I want to give them certainty that when we work together and we put political stripes aside, we cannot be stopped anywhere in the world," he added.

Ford’s letter to Carney

The premier had largely remained quiet in recent days as negotiations continued, but a letter sent to Carney on Monday and released by Ford’s office Saturday offers a clearer picture of Ontario’s position.

Ford told Carney that “no deal is better than a bad deal” that could encourage the United States to seek further concessions from Canada.

“We cannot allow arbitrary deadlines, shifting justifications or escalating tariff threats to weaken our resolve,” Ford wrote.

Ford also called on Ottawa to prepare for further escalation, emphasizing Ontario would not support removing its existing retaliatory measures without a deal that provides “significant relief” for Ontario workers, businesses and key sectors.

Carney says talks changed at the last minute

Also speaking to reporters on Saturday, Carney provided more details about why negotiations broke down.

He said the United States made last-minute changes involving the auto sector and sought to restrict Canada’s ability to pursue trade agreements with other countries.

“The Americans wanted to limit it to autos only, not include medium and heavy duty trucks which is a big change, obviously,” Carney said.

He also described the U.S. push to influence Canada’s other trade relationships as “a power play.”

Carney said Canada had been preparing for the tariffs and would now focus on strengthening the domestic economy while expanding trade with other countries.

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said when asked why it feels like today, Canada is entering a full fledged trade war.

“We’ve got the reserves. We’ve got the resilience,” he added.

Ontario wants more leverage

Meanwhile, Ford’s letter also urged Ottawa to use some of Canada’s biggest economic advantages as leverage, including electricity, energy and critical minerals.

He called on Ottawa to consider additional retaliatory tariffs targeting imports from key U.S. states, including Texas, Florida, Wisconsin and Alabama.

Ford argued that federal government should provide additional support to workers and businesses affected by the tariffs and pursue measures to make Ontario industries more competitive.

Among his requests is regulatory relief for the automotive sector, including changes to federal greenhouse gas emissions standards that Ford says could help protect thousands of jobs.

Ford’s message to Ottawa also came with a warning, Canada should not accept a deal simply for the sake of ending the dispute.

“Canadians expect governments to stand together in the face of economic threats,” Ford wrote.

“Ontario has consistently demonstrated that commitment and will continue to work with the federal government to defend Canadian workers, businesses and communities.”

GTHA mayors respond

Patrick Brown, the mayor of Brampton, Ont., also commended the prime minister’s decision not to accept a bad deal and to match the new U.S. tariffs.

“This is not a trade war that we have asked for. Unfortunately, we’re in it because of the misguided policies of Donald Trump. But it doesn’t mean we should take it lying down,” Brown said in an interview with CP24 on Saturday afternoon.

“When I hear the premier and the prime minister say ‘tariff for tariff,’ it’s our only recourse. We can’t continue to be bullied by this president.”

The mayor noted that the reported terms of the deal that included permanent tariffs on the auto sector wouldn’t have brought the jobs at the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant, which has been idling since 2023.

Last week, Unifor claimed that Stellantis was seriously considering closing and selling the plant.

“Stellantis made it clear to me that as long as there are tariffs, there was no business case for auto production in Canada, and they were leaving until tariffs were lifted. So, I’m glad the prime minister didn’t accept a bad deal,” Brown said.

“It would not have salvaged the auto sector in Canada.”

Andrea Horwath, the mayor of Hamilton, which is responsible for approximately 60 per cent of Canada’s steel output, said in her initial statement that the breakdown of negotiations is “extremely concerning” for her city’s businesses and workers.

“As a steel and manufacturing city with a significant agricultural sector, we know the uncertainty ahead will be stressful for many Hamiltonians,” Horwath said in a statement.

Horwath released an updated statement on Saturday afternoon following Carney’s news conference and said she fully agrees with the decision to reject the deal.

“Hamilton is well positioned to help lead Canada’s economic diversification, strengthen interprovincial trade and national supply chains, expand direct access to global markets, and create opportunities across our steel, advanced manufacturing, agriculture, life sciences and other key sectors,” the mayor said.

“I have reached out to the Premier, as well as business and union leaders, and will continue those conversations in the days ahead as I continue to advocate for Hamilton’s workers and businesses.”

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said in a statement that the city is ready to support Canada’s response to the new U.S. tariffs and will work with both levels of government to protect local jobs.

“These repeated tariff threats are designed to create uncertainty and weaken our resolve. But as Torontonians, we always stand up for each other. We can each do our part by buying local and supporting local jobs. We’re strong, caring, resilient, and proud to be on Team Canada,” Chow said.

items._ogDesc: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.
items.body:
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew fully supports Prime Minister Mark Carney and the federal government’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.

Speaking Saturday afternoon, Kinew commended the prime minister for standing up for Canadians and that all premiers are united with Carney.

“History will not be kind to Donald Trump. So we should never appease him and we should fight back, which is what Canada is doing today,” said Kinew. “We can fight back against Donald Trump by buying from Canadian businesses, by supporting Canadian workers and most importantly, by living up to our Canadian values.”

Late Friday evening, both Canada and the U.S. announced a trade deal had fallen apart, which resulted in 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods from the States.

Carney has since announced reciprocal tariffs will come into effect next month.

The prime minister also mentioned that trade talks disintegrated after U.S. trade representatives tried to implement last-minute changes to the deal.

“Donald Trump has certainly changed the world, but he hasn’t changed us, and we also know that Donald Trump won’t be there forever. So let’s continue extending that hand of friendship to the American people, and hopefully they will have Donald Trump and his folks see the door very quickly and we could get back to better times with our neighbours to the south,” Kinew said.

Manitoba will continue to retaliate against the American tariffs, Kinew said, by ensuring U.S. booze stays off the shelves of liquor stores across the province, as well as moving away from American businesses who apply for any tenders in the province.

The premier is also figuring out next steps to help Manitoba industries that will be impacted.

“We’ll work together with the federal government to make sure that industries that are facing this uncertainty are going to get the necessary supports,” said Kinew.

“We’re fighting for you. Donald Trump wants to take away steel, he wants to take away manufacturing jobs from our country and we won’t let them. So we’re going to stand up for our country. We’re going to stand up because we know that the red maple leaf is stronger than that guy in the red hat down south.”

Kinew also had a message for Americans, saying their cost of living is going to continue to climb under these new tariffs.

“He continues to undermine any credibility that he has on the cost of living, and the worst part about it, even the MAGA-hat-wearing American crowd should realize, is that he doesn’t care,” he said. “He only cares about making his family richer.”

Gillingham doesn’t mince words on trade war

Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham also commented on the trade war Saturday, saying there is only one group that is responsible for the latest dispute.

“It is the result of the President of the United States and his advisors continuing to follow through on his arrogant threat to try to control our country using ‘economic force,’” Gillingham said in a statement.

“I support free trade, but you can’t practice free trade when the leader of your biggest trading partner is trying to choke your economy into submission.”

Gillingham said the city will do whatever it can to help the provincial and federal governments “fight this bullying.”

The mayor is calling on all Canadians to join together and help each other prosper during this uncertain time.

As the United States slaps a 50 per cent tariff on some Canadian goods, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is calling it a violation of the CUSMA trade deal.

“Last minute changes by U.S. negotiators undermined the fairness and reliability of the deal,” Moe said in an X post on Saturday.

Moe says over the past few days, the Canadian government was working toward a deal that would have avoided new tariffs and reduced some tariffs that were previously imposed by the U.S.

“The new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on some Canadian goods are a clear violation of CUSMA and a clear indication that the current U.S. administration cannot be trusted to live up to its own trade deals,” Moe’s statement read.

In response, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada intends to retaliate and match “those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” a response Moe says Saskatchewan supports.

“In the end, the U.S. administration chose to stick with this failed economic policy, and Canada must respond accordingly,” Moe’s statement read.

“The Prime Minister made the right decision to not accept an unfair and unreliable deal, and we support the Prime Minister’s decision to enact dollar for dollar counter-tariffs on targeted U.S. products.”

items.description: An Ottawa-area distillery is redirecting its expansion plans after Canada-U.S. trade negotiations collapsed and new 50 per cent American tariffs took effect on Saturday.

items._ogDesc: An Ottawa-area distillery is redirecting its expansion plans after Canada-U.S. trade negotiations collapsed and new 50 per cent American tariffs took effect on Saturday.
items.body:
An Ottawa-area distillery is redirecting its expansion plans after Canada-U.S. trade negotiations collapsed and new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods took effect on Saturday.

Stratford-Fox Distillery had been preparing to enter the much larger U.S. market. General manager and master distiller Adam Brierley says that plan is now being reconsidered.

“A big part of our plan was to move into the United States,” Brierley said. “It’s a bigger population, the U.S. dollar is usually stronger, and we’re now reconsidering that and looking to Europe.”

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian products, including alcohol, after negotiations broke down Friday. Prime Minster Mark Carney suspended further talks and said Canada intends to respond to the tariff’s dollar for dollar.

  • Sign up now for daily CTV News Ottawa newsletters

Brierley says Stratford-Fox will instead concentrate on expanding east and west within Canada. The distillery is discussing potential listings in Manitoba, Alberta, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan, while also considering opportunities in Europe.

The company produces its whisky, vodka, gin, rum, and liqueurs locally using Ontario-grown grain. Its cardboard packaging is also manufactured in Ontario, while its glass bottles are sourced from Europe.

“We invested very early in making sure that our supply chain was as Canadian as possible,” Brierley said about the company which was founded in 2020. “I’m glad to see that that’s paying dividends now that we have all of this trade uncertainty.”

The dispute has created opportunities for the distillery within Ontario.

Before American alcohol was removed from LCBO shelves, Stratford-Fox had one product listed with the provincial retailer. Its whiskey is now available at more than 200 LCBO locations and has become the eighth-most-popular whisky in Ontario, according to Brierley.

Earlier this week, Carney asked premiers to consider returning American alcohol to provincial stores as Canada attempted to secure an agreement with Washington. With no agreement in place, Ontario has not announced any change to the current LCBO boycott.

Outside an Ottawa LCBO on Saturday, shoppers expressed support for Canada’s decision to walk away from the proposed agreement.

“I think President Trump needs to be put in his place,” said Ottawa resident Paul Fennell. “I think Carney – I believe he’s doing the right thing to make it happen.”

Carol Lenz said the latest developments have not changed her commitment to avoiding American products.

“Absolutely no interest in buying anything American if I can avoid it, and certainly not American liquor,” she said.

Despite the additional shelf space and growing interest in Canadian products, Brierley said he ultimately hopes both countries can find a path back to stable trade relations.

“I do hope that we get to a deal at some point in time,” he said. “Speaking personally, I do hope that trade relations normalize.”

items.body:
After weeks of intense talks, Canada and the U.S. have failed to strike a last-minute trade deal, meaning new 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion-worth of Canadian goods are now in effect.

Both Canada and the U.S. made the announcement in separate statements late Friday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada intends to retaliate and match “those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”

While progress has been made, Carney says it has “not been enough” and trade negotiations will now be suspended, with additional support measures coming for Canadian workers and businesses.

The prime minister also adds that “last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, called the failed talks a “missed opportunity.”

“Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week, despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market,” Greer said in a statement. “New demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days.”

According to Greer, the U.S. offered “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos and lumbers in exchange for other concessions from Canada.”

Greer also said the U.S. offered “a historic economic and national security partnership” and the announcement of formal Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) negotiations.

Last month, the White House threatened 50 per cent tariffs on a variety of Canadian goods in response to what U.S. President Donald Trump characterized as discriminatory trade policies. Namely, the U.S. took issue with provincial bans on U.S. alcohol, supply management on dairy and certain tariffs and quotas on cars imported to Canada from the U.S.

And since that threat, talks have intensified after months of little to no progress.

Trump said talks were ‘moving along’

Prior to Friday’s failed talks, Trump struck a more optimistic tone on the state of negotiations, saying they were “moving along.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, meanwhile, had told reporters Thursday that both sides were “very close.”

But in the lead up to Saturday’s deadline, two sources close to the negotiations told CTV News about some challenges with the dynamic in negotiations, particularly with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick who was involved in the final hours of talks.

As for what the deal would have included, multiple sources had previously told CTV News that Canada would have received sectoral tariff reductions for steel, aluminum and autos. Multiple premiers also said this week that Carney had asked them to return U.S. alcohol to provincial store shelves as part of the deal.

Talks described as ‘not acrimonious’

In a background briefing with reporters late Friday, a senior Trump administration official described the trade talks as “candid” but “not acrimonious.”

The official, however, would not specify on what derailed an agreement but pointed to tariffs the U.S. has imposed for national security reasons, while also indicating that “Canada was interested in additional concessions that the United States wasn’t able to provide at this time.”

When asked what will happen if Canada retaliates, the official said “we don’t anticipate retaliation. It would not be constructive.”

“If Canada does retaliate, then obviously the president will be provided with options to level out the playing field once again with respect to USMCA discussions,” the official added.

Currently, CUSMA negotiations between Canada and the U.S. have not formally begun, while talks between the U.S. and Mexico are well underway. In July, the U.S. declined to extend the existing trade pact for a new 16-year term, meaning annual joint reviews are now required.

The official also said Friday that there are no scheduled meetings between Canadian and American officials.

Premiers respond to failed trade talks

As talks intensified this week, Ontario Premier Doug Ford – who has been vocal about the ban on U.S. alcohol sales – has been relatively quiet. But in a statement on Friday, he said the “prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”

“Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before,” Ford added.

B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, also responded to the news, saying Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.”

“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” Eby added.

There is frustration, however, from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who says she is “deeply disappointed” that no deal was reached and is “urging the federal government to restart negotiations as soon as possible.”

items.body:
The collapse of trade talks between Canada and the United States, the imposition of 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods and Prime Minister Mark Carney pledging dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs triggered swift reaction from the nation’s business community.

Candace Laing, Canadian Chamber of Commerce president and CEO, called the breakdown a “body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga.”

“A whopping, non-absorbable tariff is not sustainable or viable for business,” she said in a statement. “For a small Canadian exporter operating on tight margins, this isn’t an abstract trade dispute. It means looking at your orders, your payroll and your employees and asking what you can still afford.”

Laing, who is a member of Carney’s Canada-U.S. relations advisory committee, added Americans will see their costs go up, while Canadians will see customers, investment and small businesses disappear.

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian exports Saturday, after the two countries could not reach a new deal before an extended deadline imposed by President Donald Trump earlier in the week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said he suspended negotiations and directed Canadian negotiators to return to Ottawa. He also announced Canada will retaliate with matching dollar-for-dollar tariffs.

Carney said supports for Canadian businesses and workers will be announced in the coming days.

Unifor president Lana Payne, who is also a member of Carney’s advisory committee, said in a text message the Canadian negotiators made “the right decision by walking away.”

“We can’t trade good jobs for a bad deal. And it was clear the U.S. was continuing to push for untenable concessions,” she said.

“Trump’s never-ending list of concessions, threats and economic extortion are designed to break us and own us. We need to stand together. We need to fight together.”

Dan Kelly, Canadian Federation of Independent Business president and CEO, said on social media that this new American tariff is “deeply troubling for thousands of small Canadian exporters.”

“A full 40 per cent of small exporters sell items on the new 10+ page list of items facing 50 per cent tariffs,” Kelly said.

“Many CFIB members have said this will end their U.S. sales and some have reported this will kill their businesses.”

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, said on social media that walking away from a bad deal “is the right choice for Canada.”

“The road ahead will be tough. But we’re all in this together. We must use our leverage to force Trump to back down,” she said.

“And we must focus on protecting workers and communities impacted by Trump’s trade war.”

Chris Swonger, Distilled Spirits Council of the United States president and CEO, said in a statement that continued “discriminatory treatment” of American spirits by most provinces has caused significant harm to the industry.

“We encourage policymakers on both sides of the border to pursue a negotiated solution that restores market access for U.S. spirits throughout Canada and returns spirits trade to a zero-for-zero tariff framework,” he said.

All provinces except Alberta and Saskatchewan have not been stocking American booze in response to the sectoral tariffs the Trump administration placed on steel, aluminum and autos at the start of his term.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 22, 2026.

items.description: The U.S. president said on social media that he had committed to ensuring the imported beef would be sold at 25 per cent below current market rates, making it cheaper for American consumers.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President Donald Trump speaks during a meeting with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jacquelyn Martin</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The U.S. president said on social media that he had committed to ensuring the imported beef would be sold at 25 per cent below current market rates, making it cheaper for American consumers.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump announced Friday that his administration will allow more beef to be temporarily imported into the U.S. without triggering higher tariffs, which drew swift pushback from cattle producers and conservative rural-state Republicans.

Beef prices have climbed to record highs amid a drop in the number of U.S. cattle, consistent consumer demand and limits on cattle from Mexico, where the animals are facing a flesh-eating pest. The U.S. president has also imposed 50 per cent tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter.

Trump remains under pressure to cut costs and address affordability issues ahead of November’s midterms. But ranchers, normally some of the president’s biggest supporters, are enjoying some rare profitable years and worry cheap beef imports will reduce cattle prices — and with it, the incentive to increase herd sizes.

“We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers,” Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement. “Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand.”

When asked by reporters Friday evening about criticism of the deal, Trump said, “I love the ranchers; they’ve done a fantastic job. But they admit that we need a little help, and, in order to get the prices down, so that’s what we’re doing.”

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., said in a social media post just hours after Trump announced the deal that the president’s “heart is in the right place,” but importing beef will “harm our ranching families who feed the nation.”

And Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., said that while he appreciates the administration’s focus on grocery prices, “short term policy shifts do not equal long term solutions.”

The deal, Trump said, allows up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported into the U.S. for the next 90 days without activating an “out of quota” tariff, which is a tax that goes into effect once a certain quantity of that product enters the country.

The president said on social media that he had committed to ensuring the imported beef would be sold at 25 per cent below current market rates, making it cheaper for American consumers. Trump didn’t specify which countries would import the beef while speaking to reporters Friday, but said “there are a few” and that they’ll send the “highest quality beef.” A White House official said the deal is with foreign beef exporters who have agreed to the discount on beef.

“You don’t put America first by putting U.S. cattle producers last,” U.S. Cattlemen’s Association President Justin Tupper said in a statement. “This move will weaken our markets and gamble with food safety in the process.”

The president’s announcement and other market interventions sacrifice “long-term stability for short term messaging,” Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement.

Glynn Tonsor, a professor at Kansas State University who focuses on the cattle and beef industry, said he would like to see more details about the latest deal but that his immediate assessment was that it wouldn’t have a big effect on prices

David Anderson, professor of agricultural economics at Texas A&M University, said he was skeptical other countries could redirect so much beef to the U.S. in such a short time period.

“Is that even achievable?” he questioned in a phone interview.

The White House official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a plan that has yet to be finalized, said the beef in question is lean beef trimmings that are used for ground beef production. Trump plans to sign an executive order formalizing the directive within two weeks, the official said. The administration made a push last year to buy more beef from Argentina to try to bring down prices.

The president said Friday that his plan would help grow the U.S. cattle supply, which is the smallest it’s been in decades. Some ranchers and experts said the opposite effect was more likely.

“Imports have been a major contributor to the decline in the U.S. cattle inventory,” said Bill Bullard, the CEO of the R-CALF USA, which represents independent cattle producers. “Using more imports today will exacerbate that decline and will prevent herd expansion.”

Seung Min Kim And Jesse Bedayn, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: Canada’s ban on most foreign homebuyers is set to expire Jan. 1, but economist Mike Moffatt says there is little evidence it made housing more affordable.
items.body:
Canada’s effort to make housing more affordable by keeping most foreign buyers out of the market may have failed to address the problem it was designed to solve.

The federal ban, introduced more than three years ago, is set to expire Jan. 1, and Ottawa has yet to say whether it will be extended.

But Mike Moffatt, economist and founding director of the Missing Middle Initiative at the University of Ottawa, said there is little evidence the measure had much impact.

A nationwide solution to a local problem

In interview with CTV Your Morning, Moffat said foreign investment was concentrated in pockets of the country, particularly Toronto and Vancouver, while the housing market had already begun to cool down by the time the restrictions took effect.

“This was a nationwide rule designed to address problems in two small parts of the country and probably came a few years too late to really accomplish much of anything,” he said.

Moffatt also argued the policy overlooked the role of domestic investors and existing measures designed to deal with vacant properties.

More red tape, little impact

Moffatt believes some domestic investors were also buying condominium units and leaving them empty, a problem governments had already tried to address through vacant-home taxes.

“The rules were also redundant that we had a measure in place to discourage both foreign and domestic buyers from buying a condo unit, (and) leaving them empty,” he said, adding “This really just created another set of red tape, but it didn’t really seem to accomplish a whole lot.”

Should the ban stay?

With the deadline approaching, Moffatt says letting the restrictions expire could be the simplest option.

“It’s not working particularly well, and I think it’s creating headaches for talent who wants to move to Canada but can’t find a place to live.”

But if Ottawa decides to keep the ban, he said it should be changed to allow foreign buyers to purchase newly-built homes.

“This actually creates new supply,” Moffatt said, pointing to Australia as an example with an exemption for foreign investment in new construction.

More homes, not more demand

Moffatt believes foreign investors are unlikely to return to the Canadian housing market in large numbers anytime soon, but that could change if market conditions improve in the coming years.

For Canadians struggling to buy a home today, he said the bigger issue is supply.

“We certainly need more supply,” Moffatt said.

He pointed to measures such as eliminating the HST on smaller, family-sized homes and lowering development charges as steps in the right direction.

“What they do is they target new supply, they’re not out boosting the demand for resale homes, but they’re out getting more shovels in the ground.”

And that, he says, is particularly important for families facing a shortage of these homes.

“Because we still have a housing shortage, particularly when it comes to family-sized homes .... where we’re being less comfortable raising kids,” he concluded.

items.title: Nearly 3 in 10 Canadian renters now rely on AI to find a home
items.description: Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country
items.content: <p>Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639229390796970339.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rentals.ca survey finds AI adoption now mainstream among active renters across the country
items.body:
Nearly three in 10 Canadians actively searching for a rental are now using artificial intelligence tools to navigate that process, and most of them say it helps.

Rentals.ca's Spring 2026 Renter Preference Survey, conducted between May 5 and June 14, among 1,194 active renters across Canada, found that 28.5% of respondents had turned to AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini at some point during their apartment search.

Of those 340 users, 72.6% found the experience helpful. The 70.9% majority have yet to try AI-assisted searching, but at close to 30% adoption among active renters, the behaviour has moved well beyond early-adopter territory.

For mortgage brokers, the pattern is worth tracking. A significant share of today's renters are prospective first-time buyers, and the tools shaping how they research housing are likely to carry into how they approach financing decisions.

Brokers keeping pace with housing affordability trends and rental market conditions across Canada may increasingly encounter clients who arrive at the mortgage conversation already armed with AI-generated neighbourhood comparisons and affordability estimates.

What renters are doing with AI

Among the 340 respondents who reported using AI, applications spanned the full arc of the rental search process.

Finding listings or researching neighbourhoods was the most common use at 57.7%, followed by comparing rental prices across markets at 45.5%.

Understanding lease terms and provincial tenancy rules attracted 40.2% of users, an indication that renters are treating AI as an accessible, on-demand guide to legal complexity.

Getting budgeting and affordability advice accounted for 38.1%, while drafting messages to landlords drew 33.3%.

In a competitive market, applicants are using AI to present themselves more professionally. Discussions about how Canadians are navigating digital tools and payment security risks continue to grow, the degree to which AI-assisted content is entering the borrower funnel is a dynamic the industry will need to account for.

Who is and isn't adopting

The 25–34 cohort leads adoption at 35.5%, but the generational divide is narrower than the AI narrative would suggest. Renters aged 65 and over reported AI usage at 22.8%, nearly identical to the 45–54 cohort at 22.5%.

Income predicts uptake more sharply: those earning $125,000 or more adopt at 37.9%, compared to 23.8% among renters earning under $25,000, the group that arguably faces the most acute affordability pressure.

Regionally, Toronto and Ontario lead at 29.9%, while Québec and Montréal trail at 22.7%, a gap Rentals.ca attributes partly to the predominantly English-language nature of major AI platforms.

Across all other markets, adoption is broadly consistent, with fewer than 8 percentage points separating the highest and lowest regional figures.

Meanwhile, Canadians searching for homes in the country's more affordable markets are the most likely to encounter real estate listings written by AI, according to a study by Originality.ai. Human-written ads averaged $3,037 per month versus $2,997 for likely AI-generated ones.

Brokers advising buyers would do well to encourage clients to read listings critically, verify property details in person, and consult directly with realtors on any claims that seem unusually polished or unusually vague.

items.title: The ‘heartbreaking’ crisis facing presale condo buyers is rumbling on
items.description: Real estate investors have been criticized for a gamble that backfired – but plenty of first-time buyers have also been burned, says broker
items.content: <p>Real estate investors have been criticized for a gamble that backfired – but plenty of first-time buyers have also been burned, says broker</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639229313025982717.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Real estate investors have been criticized for a gamble that backfired – but plenty of first-time buyers have also been burned, says broker
items.body:
A problem that’s gripped Canada’s two major condo markets of Vancouver and Toronto isn’t showing much sign of slowing: a surge in presale condos coming in well below purchase price, leaving many borrowers facing lost deposits, developer lawsuits, and few realistic options.

In Vancouver, the crisis is pushing mortgage brokers well beyond their traditional role, according to Lev Keselman (pictured top), managing partner at Peak Mortgage Co.

“I’ve been brokering for 20 years and I haven’t faced this before,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “It’s heartbreaking because [for clients], it’s savings spent towards leaving the deposit. They’re unable to complete. On top of walking off the deposit, they get sued by the developer.”

Scores of buyers signed presale agreements in 2021 and 2022, when the condo market was red-hot, values continued to soar and demand for rental properties remained high.

But the market’s dramatic cooldown since then has seen values plunge – meaning those buyers are suddenly faced with appraisals coming in as much as 20-25% below the original purchase price, according to Keselman, when their units complete.

That’s a gap so large that in most cases, even a conversation with the appraiser becomes academic. “At that point in time, it just becomes like a hopeless discussion,” he said.

Appraisers working on condominiums have also highlighted the challenges they’re facing and encouraged brokers and their clients to lock in an appraisal as early as they can in the mortgage process.

But options narrow quickly for buyers who signed contracts at peak prices and are now facing a completion they can’t fund. Keselman said his team tries to guide clients toward bank lenders that hold blanket appraisals, which can occasionally produce a more favourable result.

If that fails, the conversation shifts to legal counsel. “It’s ultimately referring them out to a lawyer to try to defend them against the developer,” he said. “or in some instances, maybe try to negotiate a partial refund of the deposit if possible.”

First-time buyers bearing the brunt

The fact that the presale problem is concentrated in condominiums also means many of those now caught in the completion crisis are first-time buyers who purchased without realizing what a years-long market slowdown could mean for their deal.

That’s a long way from the perception some have of the condo crisis as a fiasco only facing investors who gambled recklessly on rental units and paid the price.

Brokers aren’t just arranging financing for those first-time buyers, Keselman said – they’re also managing expectations, providing emotional support, connecting clients with lawyers and other professionals, and in some cases helping people understand that there may be no path to completion.

“A lot of times it’s just having empathy towards those clients,” Keselman said, “and trying to help them deal with the situation.”

Is the bottom in sight?

Few believe that the condo market is about to bounce back anytime soon, with no sign of a swift rebound for the sector. But Keselman believes the structural conditions for an eventual recovery are beginning to fall into place because developers are no longer committing to new condo projects in Toronto and Vancouver, which means there’s little chance of even more excess supply hitting the market.

“I think right now, there’s too much inventory, but it’s going to get absorbed,” he said. “There are ultimately a lot of the big developers on the West Coast just not starting new projects. So you’re going to have much less inventory as time passes by.”

That issue won’t resolve itself in a matter of days or weeks – but could work itself out within six to 12 months, Keselman said, as supply and demand gradually rebalance.

But until that happens, the human cost is continuing to mount. The wait for a market rebalance offers little comfort and borrowers and clients are left to navigate a situation that has little real precedent in recent Canadian mortgage history.

“I was at a bank previously during the global financial crisis and I think we dealt with a lot of those people not being able to complete at that point in time,” he said. “But it’s the first time I’ve seen it as a broker.”
